stem: Match each presentation of a breast mass to the appropriate description.

items.right: Well demarcated and circumscribed sac filled with air, fluid or semi-solid
Lumpy nodular breast tissue with tenderness that varies through the menstrual cycle.
Collection of pus that is usually red, hot, swollen and tender
Single breast nodule that is well circumscribed and demarcated, firm and mobile.

answer:
The pairings:

Breast massDescription
CystWell demarcated and circumscribed sac filled with air, fluid or semi-solid
Fibrocystic ChangeLumpy nodular breast tissue with tenderness that varies through the menstrual cycle.
AbscessCollection of pus that is usually red, hot, swollen and tender
FibroadenomaSingle breast nodule that is well circumscribed and demarcated, firm and mobile.

From 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass (its benign-lesion table).

  • Fibroadenoma - a benign neoplasm: a single nodule, well circumscribed and demarcated, firm and mobile.
  • Abscess - a collection of pus (acute inflammation, neutrophils) with warmth, redness, swelling and tenderness.
  • Cyst - a sac of air, fluid or semi-solid, well demarcated with smooth margins, collapsing when the fluid is drawn off.
  • Fibrocystic change - lumpy, nodular breasts whose pain or tenderness varies with the menstrual cycle; not a neoplasm.
note: prose key 'A=4; B=3; C=1; D=2' in the answer

stem: Rank each pathology report term from least (1) to most (5) malignant.
answer:
The pairings:

TerminologyRank (1 least to 5 most malignant)
Atypia Present, Cannot exclude malignancy3
Suspicion for Malignancy4
Atypia Present, Favour Reactive2
Positive for malignancy5 - most malignant
Negative for malignancy1 - least malignant

From 06 - Communication of the Pathology Report. When a diagnosis is not clear-cut the pathologist writes a narrative report using a graded vocabulary of malignancy risk. The lecture's scale runs positive → suspicious → atypia (cannot exclude malignancy) → atypia (favour reactive) → negative; reversed for least-to-most:

  • 1 - negative for malignancy.
  • 2 - atypia present, favour reactive: abnormal cells, but the pathologist leans benign.
  • 3 - atypia present, cannot exclude malignancy: abnormal cells with malignancy left open.
  • 4 - suspicious for malignancy: probably cancer, short of certainty.
  • 5 - positive for malignancy.

The two atypia terms are the trap: favour reactive leans benign, cannot exclude does not.
note: prose key 'A=3, B=4, C=2, D=5, E=1' in the answer; ranks are the dropdown values

stem: Match each statement to the member of the cancer care team it describes.

items.left: Perform biopsies for cancer diagnosis and play a role in removal and cancer staging.
Involved in cancer screening, symptom relief, counselling and referrals
Provide education, resources and support to help patients and families navigate the cancer journey
Helps relieve suffering and improve quality of life at any stage in a serious illness

answer:
The pairings:

StatementTeam member
Perform biopsies for cancer diagnosis and play a role in removal and cancer staging.General Surgeon
Involved in cancer screening, symptom relief, counselling and referralsPrimary Care Physician
Provide education, resources and support to help patients and families navigate the cancer journeySocial Worker
Helps relieve suffering and improve quality of life at any stage in a serious illnessPalliative care physician

From 03 - Cancer Genetics (its interprofessional management table).

  • General surgeon: diagnostic biopsy, removal and staging, lymph node dissection.
  • Primary care physician: screening, symptom relief, counselling and referrals - the lecture's wording almost exactly.
  • Social worker: counselling through education, resources and supports, and advocacy in navigating recovery.
  • Palliative care physician: relieves suffering and improves quality of life in curable, chronic or life-threatening illness - at any stage, not only at the end of life.

The near-miss for the education-and-support statement is the Indigenous health navigator, who also counsels and advocates, but the lecture defines that role as navigating the health care system. The pathologist makes the diagnosis on the tissue but does not perform the biopsy or the removal.

stem: Identify each activity as either an Activity of Daily Living (ADL) or an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living (IADL).
answer:
The pairings:

ActivityADL or IADL
AmbulatingADL (activity of daily living)
CookingIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
DressingADL (activity of daily living)
EatingADL (activity of daily living)
FinancesIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
Hygiene (bathing)ADL (activity of daily living)
Medication managementIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
ShoppingIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
Social engagementIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
TelephoneIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
ToiletingADL (activity of daily living)
TransportationIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
TransferringADL (activity of daily living)

From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment.

  • Ambulating is the A of DEATH, a basic ADL: moving from one position to another (transfers) and walking independently. It is physical self-care, not a household task that needs planning.
  • Cooking is the F of SHAFT (Food preparation), an IADL: it needs planning, sequencing and safety judgment, not just the physical ability to feed oneself. Do not confuse it with eating, which is a basic ADL.
  • Dressing is the D of DEATH, a basic ADL: selecting appropriate clothing and putting it on.
  • Eating is the E of DEATH, a basic ADL: the ability to feed oneself. Preparing the food is a different task - cooking is an IADL.
  • Finances are the A of SHAFT (Accounting), an IADL: the ability to pay bills and manage money, a cognitively demanding task of running a household rather than self-care.
  • Hygiene is the H of DEATH, a basic ADL: bathing and grooming oneself and keeping up dental, nail and hair care.
  • Managing medications is the extra M the SHAFT note adds to the IADLs: obtaining medications and taking them as prescribed. It depends on memory and organization rather than physical self-care.
  • Shopping is the S of SHAFT, an IADL: acquiring food and clothing.
  • Social engagement is not one of the named SHAFT items, but it belongs on the IADL side by the same logic: it is a higher-order activity of living in the community, not basic self-care of the body - and none of the DEATH items (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene) covers it.
  • Using the telephone is a T of SHAFT, an IADL, along with mail, internet and email.
  • Toileting is the T of DEATH, a basic ADL: getting to and from the toilet, using it appropriately and cleaning oneself, plus continence - control of bladder and bowel.
  • Transportation is a T of SHAFT, an IADL: driving or using public transport.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) can be remembered by the mnemonic DEAT(T)H: Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Transferring, Hygiene (Bathing). Instrumental ADLs are shopping, transportation, cooking, finances, telephone, medications, social engagement.

flags.title: Social engagement is not covered by the notes
flags.html:
No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

The notes' ADL and IADL lists (DEATH, SHAFT plus medications) do not name social engagement; the IADL classification follows the key and the logic of the split, not a lecture statement.

stem: Match each prescription abbreviation to its meaning.
answer:
The pairings:

AbbreviationMeaning
POOrally
BIDTwice a day
PRNAs needed
ACBefore meal
ODRight eye

From 05 - Principles of Clinical Pharmacology (its prescription abbreviations table).

  • PO - orally.
  • BID - twice a day; the frequency series is q.d., b.i.d., t.i.d., q.i.d. for once to four times a day.
  • PRN - as needed; 01 - Approach To Prescribing adds that a PRN order still needs a maximum frequency.
  • AC - before meals; p.c. is after meals.
  • OD - right eye, paired with O.S. (left eye) and O.U. (both eyes).

OD is the trap: it reads like “once daily”, but the lecture's once-daily abbreviation is q.d.

stem:
Thermoregulation is the homeostatic balance between heat dissipation and heat production.

Categorize each term below as an effector, thermoreceptors, regulated variable, or feedforward system.

items.left: Primary sensory neurons in the skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera, and brain

answer:
The pairings:

TermCategory
Body temperature at 37CRegulated variable
Primary sensory neurons in the skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera, and brainThermoreceptors
Body temperature during hyperthermiaFeedforward system
Sweat glandsEffector

From 01 - Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature. The note frames thermoregulation as a negative-feedback loop: thermoreceptors → hypothalamus → effectors, holding the regulated variable at its set point.

  • Effector: sweat glands carry out heat loss.
  • Thermoreceptors: sensory neurons activated by warmth or cold, found in the skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera and brain.
  • Regulated variable: core temperature held at about 37°C (normal 35.5-37.7°C).
  • Feedforward: body temperature during hyperthermia is left here by elimination. The note defines feedforward as the body acting in anticipation of a thermal change (e.g. responding to a cold breeze before core temperature drops).
note: prose key 'i = D, ii = B, iii = A, iv = C' (i-iv = effector, thermoreceptors, regulated variable, feedforward)

stem: Match each cause of fever with its expected timing of onset.
answer:
The pairings:

Cause of feverTiming of onset
UTIAcute
TBChronic
HIVChronic
Intraabdominal abscessSubacute
Soft tissue bacterial infectionAcute
Connective tissue disordersChronic

From In-Class - Fever. The lecture classifies fever by onset: acute (< 7 days), subacute (1–2 weeks) and chronic/persistent (> 2 weeks).

  • Acute: UTI and bacterial soft tissue infection are listed with viral infection and pneumonia.
  • Subacute: intra-abdominal abscess is the lecture's example.
  • Chronic: TB, HIV and connective tissue disorders such as SLE are listed with cancer.

The timing itself narrows the differential: a fever past two weeks shifts the search away from ordinary acute infections toward TB, HIV, malignancy and autoimmune disease.
note: prose key 'A-I; B-III; C-III; D-II; E-I; F-III' (I acute, II subacute, III chronic)

stem: Match each antibiotic class to its site of action.
answer:
The pairings:

Antibiotic classSite of action
Beta-LactamsCell wall synthesis
MacrolidesProtein synthesis
QuinolonesNucleic acid synthesis
AminoglycosidesProtein synthesis
CarbapenemsCell wall synthesis
SulfonamidesFolate synthesis

From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. The lecture groups antibiotics by the bacterial process they hit:

  • β-lactams → cell wall: bind penicillin-binding proteins and block peptidoglycan cross-linking.
  • Macrolides → protein synthesis: bind the 50S subunit.
  • Quinolones → nucleic acid synthesis: inhibit DNA gyrase, a type II topoisomerase.
  • Aminoglycosides → protein synthesis: bind 30S and cause mRNA misreading.
  • Carbapenems → cell wall: they are β-lactams, the broadest-spectrum ones.
  • Sulfonamides → folate synthesis: folate synthesis inhibitors (e.g. TMP-SMX).
note: prose key 'I-B; II-C; III-D; IV-C; V-B; VI-A'; stem's truncated 'site of' completed as 'site of action'
